analysis.one_liner: Restores the Depression-era wall separating commercial banking from investment banking.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate the Glass-Steagall separation of banking and securities firms was introduced with 5 original backers, gathered 14 cosponsors, and died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite banking law to restore key parts of the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act, which Congress repealed in 1999. It would bar insured member banks from being affiliated with firms whose main business is underwriting or selling stocks and bonds, and would stop securities-firm executives from simultaneously running a member bank. The Federal Reserve could grant limited exceptions. Banks would have had one year to unwind the affiliations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary bank depositors and taxpayers, who are protected when the deposits insured by the federal government are kept separate from risky securities trading. Community and regional banks that do not have securities arms would face competitors on a more even footing.

how_it_helps.text: Bars member banks from affiliating with firms engaged principally in issuing, underwriting, or selling stocks, bonds, and other securities, separating insured deposits from securities-market risk.
Prohibits officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving as officers, directors, or employees of a member bank, with narrow Federal Reserve exceptions.
Gives banks a one-year transition period to comply, and allows firms already in formal liquidation to wind down.

analysis.who_pays: Large universal banks that combine insured deposits with investment banking and securities underwriting would have to restructure, sell, or spin off major business lines within a year of enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big universal banks and securities arms

drawbacks.text: The bill gives banks only one year to unwind affiliations with securities businesses, which would be a large, costly restructuring for the biggest universal banks and could disrupt financial markets in the short term.

A good-faith objection: the 2008 crisis involved many institutions that were not combined commercial-and-investment banks, so supporters could not show this wall alone would have prevented it; it addresses one structural risk among several.
The Federal Reserve would retain authority to grant exceptions in 'limited classes of cases,' leaving room for the separation to be eroded in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is structural: keeping federally insured deposits away from securities underwriting reduces the chance that investment losses force taxpayers to rescue banks, a risk demonstrated in 2008. The costs fall on a small number of very large banks, though a one-year divestment deadline is aggressive and the Fed exceptions could soften the wall. The main weakness is that the bill is a single blunt fix, not a full response to the crisis.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Maurice Hinchey and five original cosponsors introduced the Glass-Steagall Restoration Act on December 16, 2009.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill, 13 Democrats and 1 Republican.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never left the committee and received no hearing or vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large universal banks that combine insured deposits with securities businesses. Because the bill died without a vote, they never had to separate those operations, and no pressure was ever placed on them in this Congress through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big universal banks, which kept their structure

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the Glass-Steagall separation of banking and securities firms on December 16, 2009.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and drew 13 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor, but it never reached a vote, so no party split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Big universal banks (commercial banks with securities and underwriting arms)
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to cut the tie between federally insured deposits and securities underwriting within a year, breaking up business structures built after the 1999 repeal of Glass-Steagall. Their interest in keeping the combined structure ran against the goal of shielding insured deposits and taxpayers from securities losses.

industries.industry: Securities underwriting and investment banking firms affiliated with banks
industries.note: Bank-owned securities units would have had to be spun off or liquidated, and securities-firm personnel could no longer simultaneously run a member bank. The bill threatens the bank-affiliated share of the securities business.

industries.industry: Community and regional banks without securities arms
industries.note: They already operate without investment-banking affiliations, so they faced little compliance cost, while competitors that combine deposit-taking with underwriting would lose an advantage. Their interest aligns with separating insured deposits from securities risk.
